# python-wrap: full reference for language models

> Everyday Python decorators that just work. Retry, cache, time out, rate limit and more. Typed, async-aware, zero dependencies.

Generated by scripts/gen_llms.py from the documentation and docstrings.

## Agent guide

python-wrap is a typed, zero-dependency resilience toolkit: retry, circuit breakers,
timeouts, rate limits, caching, bulkheads, idempotency and policies. Every decorator
works on sync functions, `async def` functions and methods.

## Find the right API before writing code

    python -m python_wrap recipe "retry http calls"   # plain-language need -> API
    python -m python_wrap api search circuit breaker  # search names and docstrings
    python -m python_wrap api retry                   # signature, params, raises, example
    python -m python_wrap api --json                  # the whole index, machine-readable
    python -m python_wrap mcp                         # the same, as an MCP server

Do not guess parameter names: check them with `api SYMBOL`.

## Prefer a policy or a preset over hand-stacked decorators

`policy(...)` puts layers in the canonical order wherever you pass them. The presets in
`python_wrap.presets` (`http_client`, `db_call`, `third_party_api`) come with timeouts,
bounded attempts, jittered backoff, a `RetryBudget` and a breaker.

    from python_wrap.presets import http_client
    users_api = http_client("users", timeout_seconds=3)

    @users_api
    def get_user(user_id: int) -> dict: ...

## Layer order (outermost first)

    observe -> validate -> fallback -> cache -> limiter -> bulkhead -> breaker -> retry -> timeout -> guard

When stacking by hand, the decorator at the top is the outermost. So:

    @circuit_breaker(...)   # counts calls whose retries were all used up
    @retry(...)             # retries each failed attempt
    @timeout(2)             # bounds each single attempt
    def call(): ...

- `timeout` goes **inside** `retry` (per attempt). A `timeout` above `retry` bounds the
  whole call; then narrow `retry(on=...)` so it does not swallow `TimeoutExpired`.
- `circuit_breaker` goes **outside** `retry`; below it, one unlucky call trips the breaker.
- `memoize` goes outside `retry` and limits: a cache hit should skip them, and failures
  are not cached.
- `rate_limit` outside `retry` spends one token per logical call.

## Idempotency rules

- Only retry operations that are safe to repeat: reads, PUT/DELETE, writes keyed by an
  idempotency key.
- Payments, e-mails, SMS, webhooks, non-idempotent POSTs, queue publishes without
  deduplication: **no retry layer**. Pass `idempotent=False` to presets (the retry layer is
  left out) and use `@idempotent(key=...)` to deduplicate repeated requests.
- `@idempotent` across processes needs a shared result store **and** a shared lease
  backend (`RedisStore(fail_open=False)` supplies a matching `RedisLock`). It cannot give
  exactly-once effects across a crash; use an outbox or database idempotency keys for that.

## What never to retry

- Programming errors (`TypeError`, `KeyError`, `AttributeError`, `ValueError` from your
  own validation): always name the transient exceptions with `on=` (or `retry_if=`);
  `on=Exception` retries bugs (doctor PW003).
- HTTP 4xx other than 408, 425 and 429 (bad request, auth, not found, conflict on a
  non-idempotent write). Honour `Retry-After` with `delay_from=retry_after_header`.
- Authentication and permission failures, validation errors, `CircuitOpenError`,
  `RateLimitExceeded` from your own limiter, `QuotaExhausted`.
- Cancellation (`asyncio.CancelledError`, `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`): python-wrap
  never retries these, do not try to.

Always bound retries with `max_attempts` or `max_time` (PW001) and share a `RetryBudget`
between callers of one dependency (PW008).

## Common mistakes

- Unbounded retries, or retries with no per-attempt timeout (PW001, PW004).
- Timeout not shorter than the retry `max_time` (PW005).
- Two retry layers (for example an HTTP client with built-in retries plus `@retry`):
  attempts multiply (PW007).
- A sync `timeout` cannot preempt code off the main thread or on Windows (PW009): poll
  `checkpoint()` in long loops, or use `async def`.
- `memoize` on a method with no bound pins every instance (PW011): use
  `per_instance=True`, `maxsize=` or `ttl=`.
- Breakers, bulkheads and rate limits are **per process** by default. Under gunicorn,
  uvicorn workers, Celery prefork or process pools, N workers allow N times the limit
  (PW012): use `RedisBreakerState`/`SQLiteBreakerState`, `RedisWindow` and lease backends.
- Calling `time.sleep` in tests: use `python_wrap.testing.fake_clock()` instead.
- Logging raw arguments: use `log_args`/`audit`, which redact sensitive names.
- Configuring logging inside library code: python-wrap never does, neither should you.

## Check your work with the doctor

    python -m python_wrap doctor package.module:policy_or_function
    python -m python_wrap doctor --non-idempotent package.payments:charge
    python -m python_wrap doctor --multiprocess --strict package.clients:users_api

In tests:

    from python_wrap.doctor import explain
    assert explain(users_api, idempotent=True).ok

Exit status 1 means an error (or any finding with `--strict`). Fix every error; review
every warning. Finding codes PW001-PW012 are listed in the docs
(features/resilience/presets-and-doctor).

Source: https://pythonwrap.readthedocs.io/get-started/

## Get started

python-wrap is a set of decorators for the problems every project meets: calls that fail, work that repeats, load that needs limiting, and code you cannot see into. This section takes you from install to a working, tested resilient function. Read the pages in this order.

## Installation

python-wrap needs Python 3.10 or newer and has no runtime dependencies. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.

### Install

=== "pip"

    ```bash
    pip install python-wrap
    ```

=== "uv"

    ```bash
    uv add python-wrap
    ```

=== "poetry"

    ```bash
    poetry add python-wrap
    ```

The package name on PyPI is `python-wrap`; the import name uses an underscore, `python_wrap`.

!!! note "Zero dependencies"
    `dependencies = []` is deliberate. Adding python-wrap to an application, or to a library you publish, pulls in nothing else. The testing helpers in `python_wrap.testing` use only the standard library too; pytest is optional.

### Verify the install

Run this in the Python you installed into. It uses a decorator, so it checks the import and that the package works:

```python
import python_wrap
from python_wrap import retry

attempts = []

@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0)
def flaky() -> str:
    attempts.append(1)
    if len(attempts) < 3:
        raise ConnectionError("try again")
    return "ok"

assert flaky() == "ok"
print("python-wrap", python_wrap.__version__, "works")
```

From a shell, `pip show python-wrap` (or `uv pip show python-wrap`) prints the installed version.

### Type checkers

python-wrap ships a `py.typed` marker and is checked with `mypy --strict`. Decorators preserve the wrapped function's signature with `ParamSpec`, so mypy, pyright and your editor still know what a decorated function takes and returns. There is nothing to configure.

```python
from python_wrap import memoize

@memoize(ttl=60)
def square(n: int) -> int:
    return n * n

result = square(4)       # a type checker infers int
assert result == 16
assert square.cache_info().hits == 0     # and knows about cache_info()
```

Decorators that add attributes to the function (for example `cache_info()`, `breaker`, `stats`) return a typed wrapper that declares them, so `square.cache_info()` type-checks.

### Logging

Importing python-wrap never configures logging. Decorators log to the `python_wrap` logger, which has a `NullHandler`, so you see nothing until you opt in. See [Logging](../features/observability/logging.md).

### Upgrading from 0.1

Version 0.2 renames and restructures some APIs. The [migration guide](../project/migration.md) lists every change with before and after code.

### Next

Build something with it in the [Quickstart](quickstart.md), or find the decorator for your problem in [Choosing a decorator](choosing.md).

### Upgrading to 0.3

Read the [0.3 migration guide](../project/migration-0.3.md) before upgrading an application.
It covers name-segment redaction, Retry-After on returned responses, hook failure
behavior, unknown external-cache counts and explicit worker lifecycle. Redis,
SQLAlchemy, frameworks and OpenTelemetry remain optional application dependencies.

## Quickstart

In about ten minutes you will take one fragile function and make it resilient, cached, observable and fast to test. Every block on this page runs as written, so you can paste it into a file and try it.

The function is a small weather client. To keep the examples self-contained there is no real network: a fake transport fails in the ways a real one does (connection errors, hangs, outages), and each step only changes the decorators on top.

### 1. Start with a plain, flaky function

Here is the starting point. The fake transport fails twice with `ConnectionError` and then answers:

```python
calls = {"n": 0}

def transport(city: str) -> dict:
    """Stands in for an HTTP call: fails twice, then works."""
    calls["n"] += 1
    if calls["n"] <= 2:
        raise ConnectionError("connection reset")
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 21}

def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    return transport(city)

try:
    get_weather("Cairo")
except ConnectionError as exc:
    print("failed:", exc)
```

One bad packet and the caller gets an exception. Most of those failures are transient, so the right response is to try again.

### 2. Add `retry`

[`retry`](../features/resilience/retry.md) calls the function again when it raises. Name the errors that are worth retrying with `on=`; anything else still fails at once.

```python
from python_wrap import retry

calls = {"n": 0}

def transport(city: str) -> dict:
    calls["n"] += 1
    if calls["n"] <= 2:
        raise ConnectionError("connection reset")
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 21}

@retry(max_attempts=4, delay=0.01, backoff=2, on=ConnectionError)
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    return transport(city)

assert get_weather("Cairo") == {"city": "Cairo", "temp_c": 21}
assert calls["n"] == 3        # two failures, then success
```

What changed: one line. `delay=0.01, backoff=2` waits 10 ms, then 20 ms, and so on between attempts (use seconds that suit your service in real code). The caller no longer sees the two transient failures.

### 3. Add `timeout`

A retry cannot help with a call that never returns. [`timeout`](../features/resilience/timeout.md) puts a limit on each attempt and raises `TimeoutExpired`, which is also a built-in `TimeoutError`.

```python
import time
from python_wrap import TimeoutExpired, retry, timeout

calls = {"n": 0}

def transport(city: str) -> dict:
    calls["n"] += 1
    if calls["n"] == 1:
        time.sleep(0.5)           # the first call hangs
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 21}

@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.01, on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutExpired))
@timeout(0.05)
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    return transport(city)

assert get_weather("Cairo")["temp_c"] == 21
assert calls["n"] == 2        # the hung attempt was cut off and retried
```

What changed: `@timeout` sits below `@retry`, so each attempt gets its own deadline. Put it above `retry` and one deadline would cover all attempts instead. Order matters; [Stacking](stacking.md) explains the rules, and step 6 hands the ordering to `policy(...)`.

!!! note "Timeouts and threads"
    On Unix in the main thread, `timeout` uses a signal timer and interrupts the call. Elsewhere it runs the call in a worker thread and stops waiting for it, but cannot stop the work. See [Timeout](../features/resilience/timeout.md).

### 4. Add `memoize(ttl=...)`

Weather does not change every second, so asking twice for the same city is wasteful. [`memoize`](../features/caching/memoize.md) remembers results by arguments, and `ttl=` makes them expire.

```python
from python_wrap import memoize

calls = {"n": 0}

@memoize(ttl=60)
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    calls["n"] += 1
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 21}

get_weather("Cairo")
get_weather("Cairo")
get_weather("Oslo")

assert calls["n"] == 2                       # Cairo was computed once
info = get_weather.cache_info()
assert (info.hits, info.misses) == (1, 2)
```

What changed: repeated calls inside 60 seconds skip the network entirely. Exceptions are never cached, so a failed lookup is tried again next time.

### 5. Protect the service with a `CircuitBreaker`

If the weather service is down, retrying every request makes things worse for everyone. A [`CircuitBreaker`](../features/resilience/circuit-breaker.md) counts consecutive failures and, after a threshold, rejects calls immediately with `CircuitOpenError` until a recovery period has passed.

```python
from python_wrap import CircuitBreaker, CircuitOpenError, CircuitState

calls = {"n": 0}
breaker = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=30, on=ConnectionError)

@breaker
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    calls["n"] += 1
    raise ConnectionError("service down")

for _ in range(3):
    try:
        get_weather("Cairo")
    except ConnectionError:
        pass

assert breaker.state is CircuitState.OPEN

try:
    get_weather("Cairo")
except CircuitOpenError as exc:
    print(f"rejected, try again in {exc.retry_after:.0f}s")

assert calls["n"] == 3        # the fourth call never reached the transport
```

What changed: after three failures the service is left alone for 30 seconds, and callers get an instant, explicit error that carries `retry_after`. Because the breaker is an object, you can share one between several functions that call the same service.

### 6. Combine everything with `policy(...)`

You now have four protections and a question: in what order? [`policy`](../features/resilience/policies.md) takes each one by role and applies them in the recommended order, whatever order you list them in.

```python
import time
from python_wrap import (
    CircuitBreaker, TimeoutExpired, memoize, policy, retry, timeout,
)

calls = {"n": 0}

def transport(city: str) -> dict:
    calls["n"] += 1
    if calls["n"] == 1:
        raise ConnectionError("connection reset")
    if calls["n"] == 2:
        time.sleep(0.5)
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 21}

weather_api = policy(
    cache=memoize(ttl=60),
    breaker=CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30,
                           on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutExpired)),
    retry=retry(max_attempts=4, delay=0.01, backoff=2,
                on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutExpired)),
    timeout=timeout(0.05),
    name="weather",
)

@weather_api
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    return transport(city)

assert get_weather("Cairo")["temp_c"] == 21     # survived a reset and a hang
assert calls["n"] == 3
assert get_weather("Cairo")["temp_c"] == 21     # served from the cache
assert calls["n"] == 3
```

What changed: the decorator stack became one named, reusable object. Apply `weather_api` to every function that talks to this service and they share one configuration. The cache is outermost, then the breaker, then retry, then a deadline per attempt, which is the order from [Stacking](stacking.md#a-recommended-order).

### 7. Observe it

Resilience you cannot see is hard to trust. [`count_calls`](../features/observability/metrics.md) keeps call, error and latency statistics on the function, and [`subscribe`](../features/observability/metrics.md) delivers an event for every retry, cache hit and breaker change so you can forward them to your metrics system.

```python
from python_wrap import count_calls, memoize, retry, subscribe

seen = []
unsubscribe = subscribe(lambda event: seen.append(event.name))

calls = {"n": 0}

@count_calls
@memoize(ttl=60)
@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.01, on=ConnectionError)
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    calls["n"] += 1
    if calls["n"] == 1:
        raise ConnectionError("connection reset")
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 21}

get_weather("Cairo")
get_weather("Cairo")
unsubscribe()

stats = get_weather.stats
assert stats.calls == 2 and stats.errors == 0
assert "retry.attempt_failed" in seen
assert "cache.hit" in seen
print(seen)
```

What changed: `@count_calls` outermost counts what the caller experienced (two calls, no errors, even though one attempt failed underneath). The event list shows what happened inside: a failed attempt, a retry that succeeded, a cache miss and then a cache hit. Every event name is listed in [Metrics and events](../features/observability/metrics.md).

### 8. Test it instantly

Retries with real delays make tests slow. [`fast_mode`](../testing/index.md) makes every wait inside python-wrap instant while retries still run, so a test that would take minutes finishes immediately.

```python
import time
from python_wrap import retry
from python_wrap.testing import fast_mode

calls = {"n": 0}

@retry(max_attempts=4, delay=30, backoff=2, on=ConnectionError)
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    calls["n"] += 1
    if calls["n"] < 4:
        raise ConnectionError("connection reset")
    return {"city": city, "temp_c": 21}

def test_recovers_after_three_failures() -> None:
    with fast_mode():
        assert get_weather("Cairo")["temp_c"] == 21
    assert calls["n"] == 4

start = time.monotonic()
test_recovers_after_three_failures()      # would sleep 30 + 60 + 120 seconds
assert time.monotonic() - start < 1
```

What changed: nothing in the production code. The delays are real in production and instant in the test. With pytest you can enable the `pw_fast_mode` and `pw_fake_clock` fixtures instead; see [Testing](../testing/index.md).

### What you built

In production code the whole client is one decorator on one function:

```python
from python_wrap import CircuitBreaker, memoize, policy, retry, timeout

weather_api = policy(
    cache=memoize(ttl=60),
    breaker=CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30),
    retry=retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.5, backoff=2, on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError)),
    timeout=timeout(5),
    name="weather",
)

@weather_api
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    ...
```

## Choosing a decorator

Find your problem, use the decorator in the second column.

### Things fail

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A network call fails now and then | `@retry(on=ConnectionError, delay=..., backoff=2)` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/retry.md) |
| I want a default value instead of an exception | `@fallback(value)` or `@fallback(handler=fn)` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/fallback.md) |
| I just want an error to go away (returns `None`) | `@suppress(KeyError)` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/fallback.md) |
| A dependency is down and I keep hammering it | `@circuit_breaker(...)` or a shared `CircuitBreaker` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/circuit-breaker.md) |
| A call can hang forever | `@timeout(seconds)` or `with timeout(seconds):` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/timeout.md) |
| The server says `Retry-After` | `@retry(delay_from=retry_after_header)` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/retry.md) |
| Retry only part of a function | `for attempt in retrying(...)` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/retry.md) |
| A whole request needs one time budget | `with deadline(seconds):` | [Resilience](../features/resilience/timeout.md) |
| A read is occasionally very slow | `@hedge(delay)` (idempotent calls only) | [Batching and hedging](../features/resilience/hedge.md) |
| Apply retry, breaker and timeout in the right order | `policy(retry=..., breaker=..., timeout=...)` | [Policies](../features/resilience/policies.md) |

### Things are slow or repeated

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same arguments, same answer, compute it once | `@memoize` | [Caching](../features/caching/memoize.md) |
| Cached values should go stale after N seconds | `@memoize(ttl=...)` | [Caching](../features/caching/memoize.md) |
| Expensive one-time setup | `@once` | [Caching](../features/caching/once.md) |
| 100 concurrent requests for the same thing | `@singleflight` | [Concurrency](../features/caching/singleflight.md) |
| An expensive attribute on an object | `@cached_property(ttl=...)` | [Caching](../features/caching/cached-property.md) |
| Run a blocking function in the background | `@run_in_thread` | [Concurrency](../features/concurrency/run-in-thread.md) |

### Too many things at once

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gather` thousands of coroutines without flooding a server | `await gather_limit(*coros, limit=20)` | [Async toolkit](../features/concurrency/async-helpers.md) |
| Apply an async function to a list, a few at a time | `await map_async(fn, items, limit=20)` | [Async toolkit](../features/concurrency/async-helpers.md) |
| Take whichever of several calls answers first | `await race(a(), b())` | [Async toolkit](../features/concurrency/async-helpers.md) |
| Call async code from a script | `run_sync(coro)` | [Async toolkit](../features/concurrency/async-helpers.md) |
| Protect a dependency from overload; fail fast when full | `Bulkhead(n, max_waiting=...)` or `@limit_concurrency(n)` | [Async toolkit](../features/concurrency/bulkheads.md) |
| Many single lookups should become one bulk query | `@batch_calls(max_size=..., max_wait=...)` | [Batching and hedging](../features/caching/batching.md) |

### Things happen too often

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reject calls over N per second | `@rate_limit(n, period)` | [Concurrency](../features/concurrency/rate-limits.md) |
| Slow callers down instead of rejecting them | `@rate_limit(n, period, block=True)` | [Concurrency](../features/concurrency/rate-limits.md) |
| One limit per user or API key | `@rate_limit(..., key=...)` | [Concurrency](../features/concurrency/rate-limits.md) |
| Several functions share one API quota | `RateLimiter(n, period)` | [Concurrency](../features/concurrency/rate-limits.md) |
| Run at most once per interval, skip the rest | `@throttle(interval)` | [Concurrency](../features/concurrency/throttle-debounce.md) |
| Wait for a burst of calls to settle, then run once | `@debounce(wait)` | [Concurrency](../features/concurrency/throttle-debounce.md) |

### I need to see what is happening

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How long does this take? | `@timing` | [Observability](../features/observability/timing.md) |
| Send durations to my metrics system | `@timing(callback=...)` | [Observability](../features/observability/timing.md) |
| Compare how fast a function is over many runs | `benchmark(func, ...)` | [Observability](../features/observability/timing.md) |
| How much memory does it allocate? | `@measure_memory` | [Observability](../features/observability/timing.md) |
| Where does the time go? | `@profile` | [Observability](../features/observability/timing.md) |
| Log the arguments (without leaking passwords) | `@log_args` | [Observability](../features/observability/logging.md) |
| Log what a function returns | `@log_return` | [Observability](../features/observability/logging.md) |
| Keep an audit trail of who called what | `@audit` | [Observability](../features/observability/audit.md) |
| Log the call stack that led here | `@trace` | [Observability](../features/observability/logging.md) |
| Count calls, errors and p95 latency per function | `@count_calls` then `func.stats` | [Metrics and events](../features/observability/metrics.md) |
| Feed retries, cache hits and breaker trips to Prometheus or OpenTelemetry | `subscribe(listener)` | [Metrics and events](../features/observability/metrics.md) |
| Put a request id on every log line | `with log_context(request_id=...):` | [Observability](../features/observability/logging.md) |

### Bad input

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Check arguments with my own rules | `@validate_args(x=lambda x: x > 0)` | [Validation](../features/correctness/validation.md) |
| `isinstance` checks on a few arguments | `@check_type(x=int)` | [Validation](../features/correctness/validation.md) |
| Enforce my type annotations at runtime | `@enforce_types` | [Validation](../features/correctness/validation.md) |

### Half-finished work

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Undo changes to `self` if a method raises | `@revert_on_failure` | [State safety](../features/correctness/state.md) |
| Register undo steps and run them if anything fails | `@transactional` / `Transaction` | [State safety](../features/correctness/state.md) |

### Maintaining and testing code

| Problem | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tests that wait on retries and backoff | `with fast_mode():` from `python_wrap.testing` | [Testing](../testing/index.md) |
| Switch retries, rate limits or caches off in a test | `disable_retries()`, `disable_rate_limits()`, `disable_caching()` | [Testing](../testing/index.md) |
| Control time in a test | `FakeClock` / `fake_clock()` | [Testing](../testing/index.md) |
| Set the same logger, retry defaults or redaction everywhere | `configure(...)` | [Configuration](../features/configuration.md) |
| Protect every method of a class | `@wrap_methods(...)` | [Developer tools](../features/devtools.md) |
| Warn callers that an API is going away | `@deprecate(since=..., alternative=...)` | [Developer tools](../features/devtools.md) |
| Return fixed data in tests or local runs | `@mock_data(...)` | [Developer tools](../features/devtools.md) |
| Reuse a stack of decorators | `compose(a, b, c)` | [Developer tools](../features/devtools.md) |

### Common recipes

??? example "Robust HTTP call"

    ```python
    from python_wrap import circuit_breaker, retry, timeout

    @circuit_breaker(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30)
    @retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.2, backoff=2, jitter=0.1, on=(ConnectionError, TimeoutError))
    @timeout(5)
    def call_api() -> dict:
        ...
    ```

    Each attempt gets its own 5 second deadline, and the breaker counts a call as failed only once its retries are used up. See [Stacking decorators](stacking.md).

??? example "Cached, de-duplicated lookup"

    ```python
    from python_wrap import memoize, singleflight

    @memoize(ttl=30)
    @singleflight
    def load_price(sku: str) -> float:
        ...
    ```

??? example "Public API with input checks"

    ```python
    from python_wrap import enforce_types, log_args, validate_args

    @log_args
    @enforce_types
    @validate_args(amount=(lambda a: a > 0, "amount must be positive"))
    def charge(account: str, amount: float) -> None:
        ...
    ```

??? example "The same thing as one named policy"

    ```python
    from python_wrap import CircuitBreaker, policy, retry, retry_after_header, timeout

    api = policy(
        breaker=CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30),
        retry=retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.2, backoff=2, on=ConnectionError,
                    delay_from=retry_after_header),
        timeout=timeout(5),
        name="api",
    )

    @api
    def call_api() -> dict:
        ...
    ```

    The roles decide the order, so listing them differently changes nothing. See [Policies](../features/resilience/policies.md).

---

Source: https://pythonwrap.readthedocs.io/get-started/async-and-methods/

## Async and methods

Every decorator in python-wrap works on `async def` functions. You use it the same way; the wrapper behaves correctly for coroutines.

### What you get

When you decorate an `async def` function, python-wrap returns an `async def` wrapper. That means:

- `inspect.iscoroutinefunction(wrapped)` stays `True`, so frameworks that check it (FastAPI, Starlette, pytest-asyncio, `asyncio.to_thread` guards) treat it correctly.
- The decorator awaits your function. It does not return a coroutine to a sync wrapper that hides it.
- Waiting uses `asyncio.sleep`, so the event loop is never blocked.

```python
import asyncio
import inspect
from python_wrap import (
    circuit_breaker, fallback, memoize, once, rate_limit, retry, singleflight,
    throttle, timeout, timing,
)

@retry(max_attempts=2, delay=0.01)
@timeout(1)
@timing
async def fetch() -> str:
    return "ok"

assert inspect.iscoroutinefunction(fetch)
assert asyncio.run(fetch()) == "ok"

for decorator in (
    retry, fallback(0), memoize, once, singleflight, timeout(1), throttle(1),
    rate_limit(1, 1), circuit_breaker, timing,
):
    async def probe() -> None: ...
    assert inspect.iscoroutinefunction(decorator(probe)), decorator
```

Methods work too, including `async def` methods; `self` is just the first argument. Read [Methods](#methods) below before decorating methods with limiters or caches.

### Per-decorator behaviour

| Decorator | What is different for `async def` |
| --- | --- |
| `retry` | Awaits the function and sleeps with `asyncio.sleep` between attempts. |
| `fallback`, `suppress` | Catch exceptions from the awaited call. The `fallback` handler is still a plain (sync) function. |
| `circuit_breaker`, `CircuitBreaker` | Counts failures from the awaited call. `breaker.call(async_func, ...)` returns a coroutine to await. State changes are lock-protected but never hold the lock across an `await`. |
| `timeout` | Cancels the coroutine with `asyncio.wait_for`, which actually stops the work. |
| `memoize`, `cache` | Caches the **awaited** result. Concurrent awaits of the same missing key share one in-flight task, so the function runs once. Cancelling one caller does not cancel the shared computation. |
| `once` | Concurrent first awaits share one task. A first call that raises can be retried. |
| `singleflight` | De-duplicates across tasks on the same event loop, using a shared task. |
| `rate_limit` | With `block=True` waits with `await`; otherwise raises `RateLimitExceeded`. |
| `throttle` | Same semantics with an `async` wrapper. |
| `debounce` | Schedules a task on the running loop. Every caller in a burst awaits the same outcome (the last call's result). Tracked per event loop. |
| `run_in_thread` | The coroutine runs with `asyncio.run` in a new thread (its own loop). The wrapper is a plain function returning a `Future`. |
| `timing`, `measure_memory`, `profile` | Cover the whole awaited coroutine. (`profile` includes event-loop work for other tasks; see [Limitations](../project/limitations.md#measure_memory-and-profile).) |
| `benchmark` / `benchmark_async` | Use `benchmark_async` for coroutine functions; `benchmark` raises `TypeError`. |
| `log_args`, `log_return`, `audit`, `trace` | Log around the awaited call. |
| `validate_args`, `check_type`, `enforce_types` | Validate at call time; `enforce_types` checks the awaited result against the return annotation. |
| `revert_on_failure`, `transactional` | Work on `async def`. `Transaction` supports `async with`, and async callbacks are awaited. |
| `deprecate` | Warns on every await. |
| `mock_data` | Works on `async def`; the awaited result is the data. |

### Calling async code from sync code

Use `asyncio.run` from a plain script or thread, as the examples in these docs do:

```python
import asyncio
from python_wrap import retry

@retry(max_attempts=2, delay=0.01)
async def job() -> int:
    return 1

assert asyncio.run(job()) == 1
```

To run a coroutine function in the background from sync code, use [`run_in_thread`](../features/concurrency/run-in-thread.md). It gives the coroutine its own event loop in a new thread and hands you a `Future`.

### Methods

Decorators work on instance methods; `self` is an ordinary first argument. Two things differ from plain functions:

- **`rate_limit`, `throttle` and `debounce` keep their state on the decorated function**, so every instance shares one limiter, one throttle window and one pending call. Split the state with `key=` (for `rate_limit`) or build the decorated callable per instance in `__init__`.
- **`memoize` includes `self` in the cache key**, so results are per instance, but the cache holds a strong reference to every instance it has seen. Set `maxsize` or `ttl` to let them go.

Both are explained, with workarounds, in [Limitations](../project/limitations.md#shared-state-on-methods). To apply one decorator to every method of a class, see [`wrap_methods`](../features/devtools.md).

### Process pools and pickling

Decorated functions pickle **by reference**, like plain functions: `pickle` stores the module and qualified name, and loading it finds the same object again. You can submit a decorated module-level function to a `multiprocessing` pool or a `ProcessPoolExecutor`, including with the `"spawn"` start method (the default on macOS and Windows). This also covers objects that are not functions, such as `periodic`, and classes decorated with `wrap_methods`.

```python
import pickle
from python_wrap import count_calls, memoize, periodic, retry

@memoize
@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.01)
def load(key: str) -> str:
    return key.upper()

@periodic(60)
def refresh() -> None: ...

assert pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(load)) is load
assert pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(refresh)) is refresh
```

<!-- skip -->
```python
# jobs.py: workers re-import this module by name, so the function must live at module level
import concurrent.futures
import multiprocessing
from python_wrap import rate_limit, retry

@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.1)
@rate_limit(10, 1)
def fetch(url: str) -> int: ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ctx = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")
    with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor(4, mp_context=ctx) as pool:
        sizes = list(pool.map(fetch, ["https://a.example", "https://b.example"]))
```

**Limiter, breaker and cache state is per process.** Each worker imports the module and builds its own decorated function, so it has its own cache, rate limiter, circuit breaker, bulkhead and call counters. Above, `rate_limit(10, 1)` allows 10 calls per second *in each worker*, not across the pool. Nothing is shared or sent back to the parent.

Objects that hold that state refuse to pickle with a clear `TypeError`: `CircuitBreaker`, `RateLimiter`, `Bulkhead`, `RetryBudget`, `Transaction`, `Policy` and `testing.FakeClock`. Create them at module level so each process builds its own. Instances whose class uses `cached_property` pickle normally, but the cached values are not pickled: the copy computes them again on first access. See [Limitations](../project/limitations.md#pickling-and-process-pools).

### Gotchas

- **One event loop per `debounce` and `singleflight` burst.** Their state is tracked per loop; do not share a debounced coroutine across loops and expect them to coordinate.
- **`rate_limit(block=False)` raises inside the coroutine**, at the `await`, not when you call the function.
- **Sync decorators on an `async def` function you wrote yourself** (a `functools.wraps` wrapper that is not itself `async def`) hide the coroutine from python-wrap's detection. Stack python-wrap decorators directly on the `async def`, or make your wrapper `async def`.

---

Source: https://pythonwrap.readthedocs.io/get-started/stacking/

## Stacking decorators

Decorators apply bottom to top: the one nearest the `def` wraps the function first, and the one at the top is the **outermost** layer, the first to see a call and the last to see the result.

```python
from python_wrap import retry, timeout

@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.01)   # outer: sees the final result of all attempts
@timeout(5)                          # inner: bounds each single attempt
def fetch() -> str:
    return "ok"
```

Order changes behaviour, not just style. A good rule: **put a decorator outside whatever it should observe or protect as a whole, and inside whatever should happen once per attempt.**

### Order matters: four examples

#### `timing` above or below `retry`

`timing` above `retry` times the whole call, including every attempt and every wait. Below it, `timing` measures each attempt separately.

```python
from python_wrap import TimingRecord, retry, timing

outer: list[TimingRecord] = []
inner: list[TimingRecord] = []

@timing(callback=outer.append)                    # one record for the whole call
@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.01, on=ValueError)
@timing(callback=inner.append)                    # one record per attempt
def flaky() -> None:
    raise ValueError

try:
    flaky()
except ValueError:
    pass

assert len(outer) == 1 and outer[0].success is False
assert len(inner) == 3
assert outer[0].elapsed >= 0.02                   # includes the two 10 ms waits
```

#### `timeout` above or below `retry`

`retry` above `timeout`: each attempt gets its own deadline. `timeout` above `retry`: one deadline covers all attempts and the waits between them.

=== "Per attempt (retry above)"

    ```python
    import time
    from python_wrap import TimeoutExpired, retry, timeout

    attempts = []

    @retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.001, on=TimeoutExpired)
    @timeout(0.01)
    def slow() -> None:
        attempts.append(1)
        time.sleep(1)

    try:
        slow()
    except TimeoutExpired:
        pass

    assert len(attempts) == 3      # three separate 10 ms deadlines
    ```

=== "Overall (timeout above)"

    ```python
    import time
    from python_wrap import TimeoutExpired, retry, timeout

    attempts = []

    @timeout(0.03)
    @retry(max_attempts=100, delay=0.01, on=ConnectionError)
    def always_fails() -> None:
        attempts.append(1)
        raise ConnectionError

    try:
        always_fails()
    except TimeoutExpired:
        pass

    assert 1 <= len(attempts) < 100   # cut off by the overall deadline
    ```

!!! warning "Narrow `on=` when an outer `timeout` wraps a `retry`"
    `TimeoutExpired` is an ordinary exception. A `retry` left at its default `on=Exception` can catch the timeout from an outer `timeout` and keep going, so the overall deadline is swallowed. Name the transient errors you want retried (`on=ConnectionError`) and the timeout passes through.

#### `circuit_breaker` above or below `retry`

Above `retry`, the breaker counts one failure per call whose retries were all used up. Below it, every single attempt counts, so one unlucky call can trip the breaker, and `retry` then sees `CircuitOpenError`.

```python
from python_wrap import CircuitOpenError, circuit_breaker, retry

@circuit_breaker(failure_threshold=2, recovery_timeout=60, on=ConnectionError)
@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0, on=ConnectionError)
def call() -> None:
    raise ConnectionError

for _ in range(2):
    try:
        call()
    except ConnectionError:
        pass

assert call.breaker.failure_count == 2     # two calls, six attempts

try:
    call()
except CircuitOpenError:
    pass
```

Usually you want the breaker **above** `retry`: "this dependency has failed N calls in a row, after retrying".

#### `rate_limit` above or below `retry`

Above `retry`: one count per logical call. Below it: every attempt counts against the limit, which is right when the limit is the remote service's quota and wrong when it protects your own callers.

### A recommended order

Outermost first. Skip the layers you do not need.

| # | Decorator | Why here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `deprecate`, `mock_data` | Warn or short-circuit before anything else runs. |
| 2 | `audit`, `log_args`, `log_return`, `timing` | Observe the whole call, including retries and fallbacks. |
| 3 | `validate_args`, `check_type`, `enforce_types` | Reject bad input immediately; do not retry or cache it. |
| 4 | `fallback`, `suppress` | Catch whatever the resilience layers below could not fix. |
| 5 | `memoize`, `once` | A cache hit skips everything below it. Exceptions are not cached. |
| 6 | `singleflight` | Concurrent cache misses share one execution. |
| 7 | `rate_limit`, `throttle`, `debounce` | Cap calls per logical request. |
| 8 | `circuit_breaker` | Counts calls whose retries were exhausted. |
| 9 | `retry` | Repeats everything below it. |
| 10 | `timeout` | A deadline per attempt. |
| 11 | `revert_on_failure`, `transactional` | Each attempt starts from clean state and undoes itself. |
| 12 | `timing` (optional second one) | Per-attempt durations. |

```python
from python_wrap import (
    circuit_breaker, enforce_types, fallback, memoize, retry, timeout, timing,
)

@timing(threshold=1.0)
@enforce_types
@fallback({}, on=ConnectionError)
@memoize(ttl=30)
@circuit_breaker(failure_threshold=5, recovery_timeout=30, on=ConnectionError)
@retry(max_attempts=3, delay=0.2, backoff=2, on=ConnectionError)
@timeout(5)
def load_profile(user_id: int) -> dict:
    ...
```

Put the same stack on many functions with [`compose`](../features/devtools.md).

### Rules of thumb

- **`retry(on=...)` should name transient errors.** With the default `on=Exception` it also retries `ValidationError`, `CircuitOpenError` and `TimeoutExpired`, which rarely helps.
- **Observers go outside, guards go inside.** An `audit` or `timing` outside the retry loop records the outcome the caller experienced.
- **Caches go outside the things that are expensive to repeat.** `memoize` above `retry` caches the final success and skips the retry loop on a hit.
- **`singleflight` goes below `memoize`.** Cache first; only a miss needs de-duplicating.
- **Decorators that hold state belong to the function.** Stacking never merges state, but see [shared state on methods](../project/limitations.md#shared-state-on-methods).
- **Async and sync stack the same way.** Every decorator preserves whether the function is `async def`, so the order rules are identical. See [Async and methods](async-and-methods.md).

---

Source: https://pythonwrap.readthedocs.io/get-started/errors/

## Errors

Every exception python-wrap raises on its own behalf derives from one base class, `PythonWrapError`. Where a built-in exception fits, the class also subclasses it, so code written with `except TimeoutError` or `except ValueError` keeps working.

All of them are importable from `python_wrap`.

### The hierarchy

```text
Exception
└── PythonWrapError
    ├── TimeoutExpired        (also TimeoutError)
    ├── RateLimitExceeded
    ├── CircuitOpenError
    ├── BulkheadFull
    ├── ValidationError       (also ValueError)
    ├── ArgumentTypeError     (also TypeError)
    └── BatchError
```

| Exception | Also a | Attributes | Raised when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TimeoutExpired` | `TimeoutError` | `seconds`: the limit that was exceeded | A call or block ran longer than its limit |
| `RateLimitExceeded` | none | `retry_after`: seconds until a call would be allowed | A rate limit is used up and the call is not allowed to wait |
| `CircuitOpenError` | none | `retry_after`: seconds until the breaker tries again | The breaker is open, so the call was not attempted |
| `BulkheadFull` | none | `name`: the bulkhead's name or `None`; `max_concurrent`: its capacity | The wait queue is full, or waiting for a slot timed out |
| `ValidationError` | `ValueError` | `parameter`: the argument name; `value`: the rejected value | An argument failed a validator |
| `ArgumentTypeError` | `TypeError` | `parameter`, `expected`, `value` | An argument does not match its expected type |
| `BatchError` | none | none | A batch function broke its output contract for one caller's item |

### Which decorator raises which

| Exception | Raised by |
| --- | --- |
| `TimeoutExpired` | [`timeout`](../features/resilience/timeout.md) (decorator and context manager), [`deadline`](../features/resilience/timeout.md) when `check()` finds the budget spent or a `timeout` starts with none left, and [`race`](../features/concurrency/async-helpers.md) with `timeout=` when nothing wins in time |
| `RateLimitExceeded` | [`rate_limit`](../features/concurrency/rate-limits.md) and `RateLimiter` when `block=False` (the default) |
| `CircuitOpenError` | [`circuit_breaker`](../features/resilience/circuit-breaker.md) and `CircuitBreaker` while open (and while half-open with no probe slot left) |
| `BulkheadFull` | [`Bulkhead`](../features/concurrency/bulkheads.md) and `limit_concurrency` |
| `ValidationError` | [`validate_args`](../features/correctness/validation.md) |
| `ArgumentTypeError` | [`check_type`](../features/correctness/validation.md) and [`enforce_types`](../features/correctness/validation.md) |
| `BatchError` | [`batch_calls`](../features/caching/batching.md), when the batch function returns the wrong number of results, a mapping without this item's key, or something that is neither a sequence nor a mapping |

`retry` has no exception of its own. When attempts run out it re-raises the last error from your function, so callers handle the same exception types with or without retries.

### Catching them

Catch the specific class when you can act on it, and `PythonWrapError` to handle "python-wrap refused or cut off this call" in one place.

```python
from python_wrap import (
    CircuitBreaker, CircuitOpenError, PythonWrapError, RateLimitExceeded,
    rate_limit,
)

breaker = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=1, recovery_timeout=30)

@breaker
def call_api() -> str:
    raise ConnectionError("down")

@rate_limit(1, 60)
def search(q: str) -> str:
    return q

try:
    call_api()
except ConnectionError:
    pass                                   # the first failure opens the circuit

try:
    call_api()
except CircuitOpenError as exc:
    assert 0 < exc.retry_after <= 30       # tell the caller when to come back

search("a")
try:
    search("b")
except RateLimitExceeded as exc:
    assert exc.retry_after > 0             # for a Retry-After header, for example

try:
    call_api()
except PythonWrapError as exc:             # one handler for every kind of refusal
    print(type(exc).__name__)
```

Because `TimeoutExpired` is a `TimeoutError`, and `ValidationError` a `ValueError`, built-in handlers still match:

```python
import time
from python_wrap import PythonWrapError, TimeoutExpired, timeout, validate_args

@timeout(0.01)
def slow() -> None:
    time.sleep(0.5)

try:
    slow()
except TimeoutError as exc:                # also matches TimeoutExpired
    assert isinstance(exc, TimeoutExpired) and exc.seconds == 0.01

@validate_args(n=lambda n: n > 0)
def sqrt_of(n: int) -> float:
    return n ** 0.5

try:
    sqrt_of(-1)
except ValueError as exc:                  # also matches ValidationError
    assert isinstance(exc, PythonWrapError)
    assert exc.parameter == "n" and exc.value == -1
```

!!! warning "Do not let `retry` swallow these"
    All of these are ordinary exceptions. A `retry` left at its default `on=Exception` retries `CircuitOpenError`, `TimeoutExpired` and `ValidationError` too, which rarely helps. Name the transient errors you want retried (`on=ConnectionError`). See [Stacking](stacking.md#rules-of-thumb).

!!! note "Catching `TimeoutError` also catches other timeouts"
    Built-in and library timeouts (`socket.timeout`, `asyncio.TimeoutError` on Python 3.11+) are `TimeoutError` as well. Catch `TimeoutExpired` when you mean only python-wrap's.

### See also

- [Choosing a decorator](choosing.md)
- [Stacking decorators](stacking.md)
- [API reference](../api/errors.md)

Source: https://pythonwrap.readthedocs.io/features/ai/agent-friendly/

## Agent-friendly tooling

python-wrap ships tools that help AI coding agents (and people) pick the right API and use
it correctly: an `llms.txt` index, a machine-readable API index, plain-language recipes, a
packaged usage guide, ready-to-copy rule files and a read-only MCP server. All of them are
generated from the docstrings, signatures and docs, so they always match the installed
version, and none needs a dependency.

### llms.txt

The documentation site serves [`llms.txt`](../../llms.txt) (an [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org)
index of every page with a one-line description) and [`llms-full.txt`](../../llms-full.txt)
(the agent guide, the key pages in full and every public signature). Point an agent at
`https://pythonwrap.readthedocs.io/llms.txt`.

Both files are generated by `scripts/gen_llms.py` from `mkdocs.yml` and the docstrings;
`tests/test_llms_txt.py` fails when they are stale.

### The API index

<!-- skip -->
```bash
python -m python_wrap api                      # every public name with its summary
python -m python_wrap api retry                # signature, parameters, raises, example
python -m python_wrap api presets.http_client  # names public in a submodule
python -m python_wrap api CircuitBreaker.reset # methods too
python -m python_wrap api search rate limit per user
python -m python_wrap api --json               # the whole index as JSON
python -m python_wrap api retry --json
```

The same data is available in Python:

```python
from python_wrap.introspect import api_index, get_symbol, search

entry = get_symbol("retry")
assert entry is not None
assert entry.signature.startswith("retry(")
assert any(param.name == "max_attempts" for param in entry.params)
assert search("circuit breaker")[0].name == "circuit_breaker"
assert any(item.qualname == "python_wrap.doctor.explain" for item in api_index())
```

### Recipes: from a need to the API

<!-- skip -->
```bash
python -m python_wrap recipe retry http calls
python -m python_wrap recipe stop duplicate emails
python -m python_wrap recipe limit llm tokens
python -m python_wrap recipe            # list every recipe
```

Each recipe names the APIs, gives a runnable snippet, the pitfalls and the docs page:

```python
from python_wrap.introspect import find_recipes

best = find_recipes("stop duplicate emails")[0]
assert "idempotent" in best.apis
print(best.render())
```

The table lives in `src/python_wrap/_data/recipes.json`. To teach it a new need, add an
entry with `need`, `keywords`, `apis` (names as printed by `python -m python_wrap api`), an
optional runnable `snippet` and `notes`, and the `docs` path. `tests/test_introspect.py`
checks that every API exists and runs every snippet.

### The agent guide

`python -m python_wrap guide` prints a short guide to using python-wrap correctly: layer
order, idempotency rules, what never to retry, common mistakes and doctor usage. It is a
file inside the wheel (`python_wrap/_data/agent_guide.md`), so it matches the installed
version and works offline.

### Rule files for your repository

Copy one of these into your project so an agent follows the rules without being asked:

| Tool | File | Copy to |
| --- | --- | --- |
